newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. deeply involved in Bosnia's post-war era.
newsitem.headline: U.S. deeply involved in Bosnia's post-war era.

text.p: The United States, which once tried to ignore the Yugoslav conflict, finds itself committed to a long-term political and military role in Bosnia after presiding over the country's post-war elections, analysts say.
Five years ago, Washington viewed the violent disintegration of old Yugoslavia as a European problem.
This month's general elections illustrated just how deeply involved the Americans have become in a country where Europeans and Turks traditionally dominated.
In the run-up to last Saturday's poll, American diplomats descended on the Bosnian capital Sarajevo to make sure the election went ahead as scheduled without violence.

It was a U.S. envoy, Robert Frowick, who made the key decisions about the election as head of the international agency supervising the vote, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Critics, including the Moslem-led Bosnian government, said the election was not held under "free and fair" conditions as required by the Dayton peace treaty.
U.S. officials, however, argued that the vote was the only way to form common institutions that could rebuild a country divided into ethnic territories.
After the vote took place without serious violence, the Americans breathed a sigh of relief. "This is a huge success for them," said one Western diplomat.
With the same nationalist parties that started the war heading towards an election victory, analysts say the United States may be confronted with a quagmire of an indefinite duration.
"This is an American muddle," said John Fawcett, deputy director of the International Crisis Group, an organisation of analysts monitoring the peace process.
"It doesn't mean they have to have lots of troops on the ground but they will be involved politically," Fawcett told Reuters. "They're stuck."
One joke circulating in Sarajevo lampoons what critics say was the real motive behind Washington's push to hold the elections by September 14.
"Do you know what the OSCE stands for?" the joke goes. "The Organisation to Secure Clinton's Election."
Postponing the elections would have meant a public pledge by Washington that U.S. troops serving in the NATO-led peace force (IFOR) would have to stay beyond their one-year mandate.
During his own re-election campaign, U.S. President Bill Clinton has avoided the subject of troop commitments after the IFOR mandate expires at the end of the year.
Military analysts say Washington will be able to reduce the number of U.S. ground troops in the NATO-led peace force next year, with Europeans taking their place.
As the leader of the NATO alliance, the U.S. military will still be involved in planning and other aspects of the mission.
As the broker and enforcer of the Dayton peace agreement, Washington is saddled with steering Bosnia towards reconciliation and away from wartime divisions.
Washington has already committed itself to providing economic aid as well as military assistance to the Bosnian government which suffered from the effects of an arms embargo during the 43-month war.

American officials hope the "train and equip" arms programme will create military parity in the region as well as ensure that Sarajevo chooses to build ties with the West instead of with Islamic countries such as Iran.
U.S. diplomats say Washington became involved in the Balkans initially for "moral reasons" to oppose ethnic cleansing campaigns and the separatist Serb siege of Sarajevo.
After negotiating the peace accord and deploying peacekeeping troops, Washington's leadership role is now at stake.
"We have put a lot of prestige on the line," said one U.S. diplomat. "We have to protect our investment."
European countries have tended to step back and let the Americans take the lead since Washington negotiated the peace agreement in Dayton, Ohio last November.
If the peace process collapses, it will be the United States which will have to clean up the mess, said European diplomats. "Now it's their turn," said one.
Eventually, American officials say, Bosnia's ethnically divided entities will be reunifed through economic necessity.
But some analysts say that Washington, by shying away from a strict enforcement of the peace treaty's provisions for short- term goals, could end up with long-term problems.
"This will be a much more complex and volatile version of Cyprus," Fawcett said.
